name: Battle of Poitiers (1356)
info: An Anglo-Gascon army under Edward, the Black Prince, defeated a larger French army under King John II south of Poitiers in 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, and captured the king, which led to a truce and the Treaty of Brétigny.

facts.place: On a wooded hill in the Forêt de Nouaillé, 5 miles (8 km) south of Poitiers, in western France
facts.sides: Anglo-Gascons under Edward, the Black Prince, generally considered by modern historians to number 6,000 (some contemporary accounts give 4,800 or 5,000); French under King John II, between 14,000 and 16,000
facts.outcome: The French were defeated and John II was captured with his youngest son Philip and between 2,000 and 3,000 men-at-arms. The Anglo-Gascons withdrew to Gascony with their prisoners.

t: The Anglo-Gascons, about 6,000 by modern estimates, held a prepared position and beat a French army of between 14,000 and 16,000, almost all of whom fought on foot.

The battle was fought in four French attacks, and the last was broken when a small mounted force of 160 men sent round the flank appeared behind the French, who believed themselves surrounded and fled.
King John II was captured, and the Treaty of Brétigny of 1360 ceded vast areas of France to England and ransomed him for three million gold écu, though the French resumed the war in 1369.
dyk: The French sacred banner, the Oriflamme, was unfurled in the last attack, which signalled that no prisoners were to be taken, yet the Anglo-Gascons were eager to take the French elite prisoner for ransom and many were captured.
ev: Philip VI's Great Council takes back the lands held by Edward III in France, which begins the Hundred Years' War
The Black Prince sets out on a chevauchée from Bordeaux to Narbonne and back
The Anglo-Gascon army marches north from Bergerac and devastates the countryside
The Anglo-Gascons rout part of the French rearguard near Savigny-Lévescault
The Anglo-Gascons repel three French attacks and win the fourth, and King John II is captured
A truce of two years is agreed and the Black Prince takes John to London
The Treaty of Brétigny cedes large areas of France to England and ransoms John

sections.background:
Since the Norman Conquest of 1066 English monarchs had held lands in France, which made them vassals of the kings of France. By the early fourteenth century the only significant French possession left to them was Gascony, which mattered out of proportion: the duty on wine from Bordeaux totalled more than all other English customs duties combined. On 24 May 1337 Philip VI's Great Council agreed that Edward III's lands in France should be taken back, on the grounds that he had broken his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the Hundred Years' War.

Edward III could spare few resources for Gascony, whose people could usually field 3,000 to 6,000 men. Calais fell to the English in August 1347 and the Truce of Calais followed, partly because both countries were exhausted financially. The Black Death, estimated to have killed a third of the population of Western Europe, halted the fighting until 1350. A treaty negotiated at Guînes was signed on 6 April 1354, but John II, who succeeded Philip, decided not to ratify it after sentiment in his council turned against its terms, and from the summer of 1355 both sides were committed to full-scale war.

In 1355 Edward's eldest son, Edward of Woodstock, later known as the Black Prince, took the Gascon command and reached Bordeaux on 20 September with 2,200 English soldiers. Gascon nobles brought him to between 5,000 and 6,000. On 5 October he set out on a chevauchée, a large-scale mounted raid, as far as Narbonne and back, returning on 2 December. No territory was captured, but enormous economic damage was done to France.
sections.forces:
Modern historians generally consider the Anglo-Gascon army to have numbered 6,000: 3,000 men-at-arms, 2,000 English and Welsh longbowmen and 1,000 Gascon infantry, many of them with crossbows or javelins. Some contemporary accounts give 4,800 or 5,000. All rode, but all or nearly all dismounted to fight. They stood in three divisions. Thomas, Earl of Warwick, held the left with about 1,000 men-at-arms and about 1,000 archers. William, Earl of Salisbury, held the right with the same. The Black Prince commanded the centre of about 1,000 men-at-arms and 1,000 Gascon infantry, held back behind the others as a reserve. Each division was four to five men deep.

The French army numbered between 14,000 and 16,000: 10,000 to 12,000 men-at-arms, 2,000 crossbowmen and 2,000 other infantry. Almost all fought on foot, except two small groups of mounted knights, 300 or 500 in all, led by the marshals Arnoul d'Audrehem and Jean de Clermont. There were four divisions. The first, under the constable Walter, Count of Brienne, included 200 Scottish men-at-arms under William Douglas and most of the infantry and crossbowmen. The second, of 4,000 men-at-arms, was led by the Dauphin Charles, aged 19, and Peter, Duke of Bourbon. The third, of about 3,200, was led by John's brother Philip, Duke of Orléans. John himself commanded the last, of 2,000 men-at-arms and an uncertain number of crossbowmen.

On 18 September the Anglo-Gascons took a position 5 miles south of Poitiers on a wooded hill in the Forêt de Nouaillé and prepared it for defence with pits, trenches and barricades. They were confident that on ground of their choosing they could defeat a larger French force. Their food was almost exhausted and they could not find enough water for their horses.
sections.course:
The French drew up about 500 yards from the English just after dawn. After about two hours they saw movement among the English and took it for a withdrawal. Modern scholars debate whether it was wagons moving to the rear, a staged withdrawal or a feint. The leaders of the first French division ordered an advance. Audrehem's cavalry attacked Warwick's division, but the archers stood at the edge of a marsh that kept the horsemen from them, and they turned their fire on the crossbowmen. Audrehem was captured. On the right Clermont's cavalry reached a gap in a hedge and was forced back with heavy losses; Clermont and Brienne were killed.

The second French division, 4,000 strong, then attacked through the hedge, with hand-to-hand fighting for two hours. Bourbon was killed and the Dauphin's standard-bearer captured, and the Dauphin was withdrawn from the front. His division withdrew in good order. Half of Orléans's third division marched away, and three of John's four sons left the field; the rest made a feeble attack that was easily repelled.

John's fourth division, probably about 4,000 men-at-arms with crossbowmen, advanced on foot with the Oriflamme unfurled. The Anglo-Gascons, exhausted and short of arrows, sent about 160 mounted men under the Captal de Buch round the French flank, and the Black Prince ordered a general advance. The French slowly gained the upper hand until men of Warwick's division returned from pursuit and the Captal de Buch's force struck the French rear. Some Frenchmen ran, others followed and the division fell apart. Those around John were forced into a loop of the River Miosson and surrounded. John and his son Philip surrendered.
sections.aftermath:
Frenchmen who fled soon after the Captal de Buch arrived mostly reached their horses. Many fled towards Poitiers, whose citizens closed the gates and manned the walls, and the mounted Anglo-Gascons caught and killed them outside the gate. It was evening before the last Anglo-Gascons returned with their prisoners.

According to different modern sources 2,000 to 3,000 French men-at-arms and either 500 or 800 common soldiers were taken prisoner. They included the king, his youngest son, the archbishop of Sens and one of the two marshals. About 2,500 French men-at-arms were killed, with 3,300 common soldiers according to English accounts or 700 according to French ones. The dead included the Duke of Bourbon, the constable, the other marshal, the Bishop of Châlons and the standard-bearer Geoffroi de Charny. The Anglo-Gascons reported only 40 to 60 killed, of whom 4 were men-at-arms.

The Anglo-Gascons buried their dead and paroled some prisoners, then resumed their march on 21 September, slowly, laden with plunder. They entered Libourne on 2 October, and about two weeks later the Black Prince escorted John into Bordeaux. A truce of two years was agreed in March 1357. In April the Black Prince sailed for England with John and landed at Plymouth on 5 May, and they were received rapturously in London.
sections.sources:
Contemporary chroniclers on both sides recorded the battle. A French chronicler called the second attack more amazing, harder and more lethal than the others, and an English account described men fighting frenziedly. Their figures differ. Some contemporary accounts give the Anglo-Gascon army as 4,800 or 5,000 where modern historians say 6,000, and English accounts count 3,300 common French soldiers dead where French ones count 700. The Anglo-Gascon dead are reported as only 40 to 60, which Peter Hoskins calls improbably low.

Much of the detail rests on what these accounts leave open, and modern historians dispute it. The movement among the English that began the fighting has more than one explanation. The reasons for Orléans's departure are contradictory: official French accounts that John ordered him to take the princes to safety were widely disbelieved and rumoured to have been invented. It is unclear whether the Anglo-Gascons pursued after the second attack. A chronicler's report that all the Anglo-Gascon men-at-arms remounted is generally discounted. Whether Audley led a charge at the king is uncertain, and the numbers in it run from 4 to 400.

Historians also differ on whether the French or the Anglo-Gascons had more men at the last stage, and on the Black Prince's sincerity in the negotiations, since Edward III had given him leave to make a truce on his own authority. A computer analysis by Warsaw University of Technology in 2017 found that heavy bodkin arrows could penetrate typical plate armour of the time at 250 yards.
sections.legacy:
Clifford Rogers calls the Black Prince's chevauchée the most important campaign of the Hundred Years' War. After Poitiers English and Gascon forces raided widely across France against little or no opposition, and with no effective central authority France dissolved into near anarchy. A peasant revolt, the jacquerie, broke out in northern France in the spring of 1358 and was bloodily put down in June.

Negotiations to free John were protracted. The First Treaty of London of May 1358 lapsed because the French government could not raise the first instalment of the ransom, and the Second Treaty of London was rejected by the Dauphin and the Estates General in May 1359. After a further campaign by Edward III in northern France, the Treaty of Brétigny was agreed by 8 May 1360. Vast areas of France were ceded to England, to be ruled by the Black Prince, and John was ransomed for three million gold écu. Rogers states that Edward gained a full third of France in full sovereignty, his original war aims and much more. Sixteen senior nobles captured at Poitiers were released with it.

The peace seemed to end the war, but large-scale fighting broke out again in 1369. The war did not end until 1453, with a French victory that left only Calais in English hands.

summary: At Poitiers on 19 September 1356 about 6,000 Anglo-Gascons under the Black Prince held a prepared position against a French army of between 14,000 and 16,000, and captured King John II. The Treaty of Brétigny followed in 1360, but the French resumed the war in 1369.

notes: The article has no sources or legacy section (its Notes, Citations and Sources headings are empty), so 'sources' is built from the chroniclers and historians quoted in the text, and 'legacy' from the Peace section and Rogers.
One paragraph in the Fourth attack ('Then the standards wavered ... wretched bodies') is an unattributed, gory, partly garbled quotation; left out.
The article gives the Anglo-Gascon dead as 40 to 60 (4 men-at-arms) and also 'about 40 men-at-arms' plus an uncertain larger number of bowmen; I kept the 40 to 60 with Hoskins's doubt.
French prisoners: 2,000 to 3,000 men-at-arms and 500 or 800 common soldiers; the lead says 1,500 or 3,800 common infantry killed or captured; I used the casualties section's figures.
The 'Notes/Citations' do not name chroniclers; I did not name any.
